title: Europe opens bidding for seven AI ‘gigafactories’ in a €30bn bid to catch up

content_html:
The European Commission has opened the bidding to build up to seven AI “gigafactories,” vast computing hubs meant to give the bloc the raw power to train frontier AI models without depending on the United States.

The call for tenders, launched today, is pitched as a roughly €30 billion effort to close the gap with American and Chinese AI.

The structure is a public-private split. Brussels and member states would put in about €10 billion between them, with the other €20 billion expected from private investors, on the bet that state money can crowd in the capital these projects need.

The scale is deliberately enormous. Each gigafactory would house at least 100,000 cutting-edge AI chips, making it roughly four times more powerful than the largest data centres running in the EU today, and together they would more than double the bloc’s AI compute.

The “gigafactory” name is a deliberate step up. Europe already funds a network of 19 smaller “AI factories” attached to its supercomputers, but the new sites are meant to be an order of magnitude larger, built to train the kind of frontier models that today only a handful of US and Chinese labs can afford.

The appetite is clearly there. An earlier expression-of-interest round drew 76 responses from consortia across the continent, with ten countries, including Germany, France, Italy, Spain, and Poland, lining up to host, and France already signalling it will go it alone.

The reasoning is competitive anxiety. Europe has watched the US and China pour money into AI infrastructure while its own firms rent compute from American clouds, and Henna Virkkunen, the Commission’s tech-sovereignty chief, called that raw scale of computing power “a strategic necessity.”

The ambition, though, runs ahead of the cheque. Only about €1 billion of Brussels’ share is actually committed; the rest depends on the EU’s next long-term budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework, which has not been agreed.

A senior official said as much, unusually plainly. “We cannot pre-empt the decisions about the next MFF,” the official told reporters, describing the sum as a “best estimate” of what might be available rather than money in hand.

The timeline is tight against that uncertainty. Construction is meant to begin in early 2027 and the first gigafactories to come online by mid-2028, a schedule that assumes budgets, sites, and supply chains all fall into place.

History suggests caution. The gigafactory plan was first floated in early 2025 and has since slipped repeatedly, with delays that frustrated some of the very partners the Commission now needs to build the things.

There is also an awkwardness at the heart of the sovereignty pitch. The chips that would fill these European gigafactories will overwhelmingly come from Nvidia, AMD, and Qualcomm, all American, which means the bloc would be buying its independence from the companies it wants independence from.

Energy is the other constraint. European electricity costs two to three times what it does in the US or China, and data-centre power is already a limiting factor that no amount of subsidy can quickly wish away.

Critics have questioned the whole model. Some argue that renting sovereign-branded capacity built on foreign-owned hardware reinforces an illusion of independence rather than delivering it, and that Europe’s real gap is in chips and models, not buildings.

The counter is that infrastructure is a start, not a finish. Compute alone will not conjure a European OpenAI, but without it the continent’s startups have nowhere to train at scale, which is the gap the Commission is trying, expensively, to fill.

The Commission’s answer is that you have to start somewhere. Public funders would get a proportional share of the compute for research and public projects, and the hope is that building the infrastructure draws the talent, the startups, and eventually the chipmaking toward Europe.

For now, the door is open and the money is mostly notional. Firms can bid to build Europe’s AI future, on the understanding that the continent has announced €30 billion of ambition and secured, so far, about a thirtieth of it.

content_html_zh:
欧盟委员会已开始招标建设最多七个人工智能“超级工厂”，这些巨大的计算中心旨在赋予欧盟在不依赖美国的情况下训练前沿人工智能模型的原始力量。

今天启动的招标预计耗资约 300 亿欧元，以缩小与美国和中国人工智能的差距。

该结构是公私分离的。 布鲁塞尔和成员国将投入约 100 亿欧元，另外 200 亿欧元预计将来自私人投资者，押注国家资金可以筹集这些项目所需的资金。

规模故意很大。 每个超级工厂将容纳至少 100,000 个尖端人工智能芯片，其性能大约是欧盟目前运行的最大数据中心的四倍，加起来将使欧盟的人工智能计算量增加一倍以上。

“超级工厂”这个名字是有意为之的。 欧洲已经资助了一个由 19 个与其超级计算机相连的小型“人工智能工厂”组成的网络，但新站点的规模要大一个数量级，旨在训练目前只有少数美国和中国实验室能够负担得起的前沿模型。

食欲显然就在那里。 较早的一轮意向书吸引了来自整个非洲大陆财团的 76 份回应，德国、法国、意大利、西班牙和波兰等 10 个国家排队主办，法国已经表示将单独行动。

原因是竞争焦虑。 欧洲目睹了美国和中国向人工智能基础设施投入大量资金，而欧洲自己的公司则从美国云中租用计算能力，欧盟委员会技术主权负责人 Henna Virkkunen 称这种计算能力的原始规模是“战略必要性”。

然而，雄心壮志先于支票。 布鲁塞尔实际承诺的份额中只有约 10 亿欧元；其余的取决于欧盟的下一个长期预算，即多年期金融框架，但该框架尚未达成一致。

一位高级官员异常直白地说了同样的话。 这位官员告诉记者：“我们无法预先做出有关下一次多批次融资的决定。”他将这笔金额描述为对可能可用资金的“最佳估计”，而不是手头的资金。

由于这种不确定性，时间安排很紧迫。 建设计划于 2027 年初开始，第一批超级工厂将于 2028 年中期上线，这一时间表假设预算、场地和供应链都已到位。

历史表明要谨慎行事。 该超级工厂计划于 2025 年初首次提出，此后一再推迟，其延误让委员会现在需要建设这些工厂的一些合作伙伴感到沮丧。

主权争议的核心也存在一个尴尬之处。 这些欧洲超级工厂的芯片绝大多数将来自英伟达、AMD 和高通，这些公司都是美国公司，这意味着欧盟将从其想要独立的公司那里购买独立性。

能源是另一个限制因素。 欧洲的电力成本是美国或中国的两到三倍，而数据中心电力已经成为一个限制因素，无论有多少补贴都无法很快消失。

批评者对整个模型提出了质疑。 一些人认为，租用建立在外资硬件上的主权品牌产能只会强化独立的幻觉，而不是实现独立，欧洲的真正差距在于芯片和模型，而不是建筑物。

相反，基础设施只是一个开始，而不是结束。 仅靠计算并不能创造出欧洲开放人工智能，但如果没有计算，欧洲大陆的初创公司就没有地方进行大规模培训，而这正是欧盟委员会正在花费巨资试图填补的空白。

委员会的答案是，你必须从某个地方开始。 公共资助者将获得一定比例的用于研究和公共项目的计算份额，希望基础设施的建设能够吸引人才、初创企业，并最终将芯片制造吸引到欧洲。

目前，大门是敞开的，资金主要是名义上的。 企业可以竞标建设欧洲的人工智能未来，前提是欧洲大陆已宣布了 300 亿欧元的雄心壮志，并且迄今为止已落实其中约三十亿欧元。
